utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please be seated. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-95-13/1-PT, the Prosecutor of the Tribunal against Veselin Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SOLLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm familiar with the courtroom, forgive the delay on pressing the button. I'm assigned counsel today for this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. SOLLEY
utterances.text: -- for this defendant. But it's important, I think, that I tell you what the situation is. The defendant -- three lawyers arrived today from Belgrade. For many days now they have been taking instructions, it would appear, from this defendant in some form or another. They tell me that about nine days ago they sent all their credentials to the administration here so that they could be checked out, ready to become this defendant's counsel for the hearing today. Indeed, so confident were they that things had gone smoothly according to the proper course that they at their considerable expense attended today directly from Belgrade. It turns out for reasons which we can't get to the bottom of and probably can't be got to the bottom of today, the administration has not been in a position to be able to check their credentials. This defendant has, as one may understand, considerable faith in these representatives from Belgrade. Without discourtesy to me, he has no particular faith in me for obvious reasons: He doesn't know me. If it be -- and I'm not suggesting it is -- but if it be the fault of the administration in some respect or other that the lawyers he want are not properly accredited, if it be a failure on their part, then of course that must not reflect upon his shoulders in any way, and he ought to be put in a position where he can have assigned counsel of his choice, if that is the position that finally obtains, once they've been investigated. And so we're at a stage today where he tells me - and therefore I tell you - that he will not in any way respond to the position he finds himself in because, from his point of view, as you may understand, he thinks because of a failure of the administration, counsel representing him properly haven't yet been checked through and aren't in a position, as it were, to my side along this bench. Now, that may be a reasonable position. One doesn't know it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely it could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. SOLLEY
utterances.text: Therefore --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But so far I've only heard one side of the story.

utterances.speaker: MR. SOLLEY
utterances.text: And therefore, what I am proposing is, rather than proceed today, recognising as I do that it is something of a formality today, may I propose that these proceedings be adjourned for seven days so that the position can become clear as to these other counsel. If they are to be assigned to him properly, then all will be very smooth next week. In the context of what is to come over the next months, the week will not be a serious delay. But if it turns out that the administration here should have checked or could have checked and haven't, then to proceed today may be thought to be perhaps a little unnecessary in the context of the whole time frame. I have clear instructions that he does not wish to, not disrespect -- not out of disrespect to you, Your Honour, but he does not wish to appear and to take any part in proceedings where the lawyers of his choice are not present. He recognises -- forgive me. He recognises that his freedom of choice is fettered and is fettered by the Rules and regulations and the authorities of this Court, but we're not in the position yet where, as it were, the bureaucracy has gone through that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand. I understand that. But before I respond to you, I notice that Ms. Martinez is still here. Could I have an update on the position as regards the accused's proposal that three lawyers that haven't been mentioned by name, but I suppose you are aware of their existence, what the position is and what the expectations are?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARTINEZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think I can then use Mr. Solley, who comes from a jurisdiction where barristers usually know exactly how to handle such situations, and I will rely entirely on you, Mr. Solley, for your assistance. But before I do so and before I take a decision, believe me, I want to know exactly what the position is, because this Tribunal is bound by its own Rules and those Rules have to be observed. You all know that the right to be assisted by counsel does not mean that you have a right to bring here a dozen lawyers to defend you and expect the Tribunal to pay for them too. So let's take it up from there. For the time being, I think you've been extremely reasonable and moderate in your submissions. I will hear what Ms. Martinez has to say and then we'll take it up from there. If it is necessary to postpone, we will postpone. Don't worry. Yes, Ms. Martinez.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARTINEZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There are indeed two lawyers who came today from Belgrade. I wasn't here last week, so I don't -- I'm not in a position to tell you what happened with the credentials, but I checked with my office and no one has seen those papers. And all I can say at the moment is that in principle -- these two lawyers, none of them speak an official language of the Tribunal, so they are not, in principle, qualified according to the Rules. We could make an exception in the interest of justice, but obviously we would need some time to -- to review the credentials and see whether it is appropriate to do so. It's why we considered that it could be the best for the accused to appoint a qualified counsel just for the purpose of the Initial Appearance today.

utterances.speaker: MR. SOLLEY
utterances.text: May I, I hope helpfully, respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SOLLEY
utterances.text: Because of the unfortunate situation where Ms. Martinez was not here last week --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SOLLEY
utterances.text: -- as I said, I think, in my remarks, the authoritative position about this can't be determined. So it may be that in some way wires have gone crossed, and I think one ought to make --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's possible --

utterances.speaker: MR. SOLLEY
utterances.text: One ought to make that assumption. Secondly, since there is the circumstance which has been set out, namely that even if they don't speak English or French, there can be an exception made in the interest of justice, that too allows a door to be opened. And because there are those two caveats to the position, Your Honour, I would respectfully suggest that rather than proceed today and in circumstances where quite a lot of difficulty may be presented, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Those don't -- those don't bother me in the least, believe me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SOLLEY
utterances.text: Yes. I, too, have many, many years' experience of difficult situations with recalcitrant defendants. A few days' grace may be a very well-oiled solution to what today may be an intractable problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. What I'm going to do is I'm going to suspend the sitting for 15 minutes. Yes, Madam Registrar. I'm going to suspend the sitting for 15 minutes. And the following persons have got these specific tasks to play: Number one: Ms. Martinez, you will check thoroughly with your department, with your office, what the situation is with regard to the credentials, whether they were filed, when they were filed. And I don't want any justification in case they haven't been gone through and verified, because I know that you are the head of the department and if you weren't here and no one did go through them thoroughly, I will certainly not put any blame on you. But I will want to know how fast you would be in a position or how early you would be in a position to come back to us with a decision; come back to us or to the accused. That's number one. Mr. Wubben, I would like you to consult your superiors on whether there is an objection on the part of the Prosecution that the Initial Appearance be postponed to some other day next week, with the understanding that by that time a decision would have been taken by Ms. Martinez or whoever is responsible for -- for the Registrar. And the final person with an important task is you, sir. I would like you to go back to your client and explain to him that the right to counsel does not mean that he can dictate to the Tribunal how many lawyers and who can represent him. We've got our own Rules, our own restrictions, and we have to abide by those. That's number one. Number two, you need to explain to him also that I -- in me he will find the best defence. I'm not saying that you will not defend him well, but I am -- want you to explain to him that the person who will look at a hundred per cent level, constantly and at all time will be myself as a Pre-Trial Judge until we come to the trial stage. And I can promise him that his interests, his rights, will be protected at all costs by me as the Pre-Trial Judge. But that also means - it's not a question of respect or disrespect - that if I say that he has to be here to answer questions, he needs to be here. I will caution him that he has the right to remain silent. But if I say he has to come in here, he will have to come in here. And if he doesn't come here on his two feet, I'll make sure that he is brought in here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SOLLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hope we won't get to that stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope so. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. SOLLEY
utterances.text: I would like to make submissions to you about what I regard as the -- what I would submit to you, respectfully, as the unlawfulness of that course in due course, but we may not get to that bridge. I do want you to know that counsel, of course, are not meant to have personal views, and so I have to tread carefully. But since you asked me to put the first point, I -- about counsel of choice, it would be right for me to say that I don't regard this as being truculence that brings him into this position today, just sheer bloody-mindedness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, no. It's not capricious at all. I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SOLLEY
utterances.text: It could happen. But it is not the position here today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SOLLEY
utterances.text: I want Your Honour to know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand that. And I also understand the position in which you find yourself at. That's why I'm telling you you don't just have my sympathy but you also have my full understanding and support.

utterances.speaker: MR. SOLLEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I want to show publicly my appreciation for your cooperation, Mr. Solley, because that is extremely useful. So I will suspend the sitting for 15 or 20 minutes and which -- during which time, particularly, Mr. Wubben, I want some kind of categoric feedback from the Prosecutor, because if there is an insistence that we proceed today, then much depends on what Ms. Martinez will tell me. The sitting is suspended for 20 minutes. Thank you. --- Break taken at 3.57 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll reconvene. Ms. Martinez, I'm going to start with you. Have you consulted your superior -- your immediate superior and found out as to what happened exactly and what the situation is?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARTINEZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have found out that we have indeed received the documents last Tuesday. My office received the documents with a request for a visa for these two lawyers. Our practice usually is that we don't recognise any power of attorney if it's not directly coming from the accused. So we always wait until the accused comes and then we meet with the accused and the lawyers and we get this power of attorney together with the declaration of means and all that. I must say that it's unfortunate - I don't know what happened - but usually we should have contacted these lawyers to find out whether they were indeed duly qualified, especially because we always check whether they speak an official language. According to the -- because we have only received a CV for one of them, the other one, we don't have any CV, and the one we have received is not actually completed. We need further information on the criminal law experience. From the CV, we can't really see whether they speak English or not, so now we found out that none of them speaks actually English, an official language of the Tribunal. So in principle, as I said before, they are not qualified, according to Rule 44(A) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, so we only could make an exception in the interest of justice and we only do that in very exceptional circumstances, when we have really very compelling reasons to -- in the interest of the accused. What can I say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, Ms. Martinez. I think your client should be here to listen to all this. Please. I will suspend again. Go and tell him I want him in here. We will not start the proceedings proper but I want him in here to know exactly what is happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. SOLLEY
utterances.text: You needn't rise, Your Honour. I have spoken to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SOLLEY
utterances.text: And in order to avoid any kind of physical problem, if you order him to be in court, he will be in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So I'm making an order. We will not proceed because, from what I've heard now, it's enough justification for me to postpone the basic part of the Initial Appearance until some later point in time. But I want him to be present.

utterances.speaker: MR. SOLLEY
utterances.text: With respect, I couldn't agree more with you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. So please --

utterances.speaker: MR. SOLLEY
utterances.text: Can I just mention this: I gather there were some photographers there, and I don't suppose they'll come in now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not while I am sitting. Definitely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SOLLEY
utterances.text: Good. Because since we don't know the case yet that we have to meet, I'm concerned about issues of identification. But I needn't even mention that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. There is, Mr. Solley, a -- an order which we sign in every Initial Appearance, and that's an order authorising the taking of photographs and for the release of audiovisual records. But since we haven't really started with the Initial Appearance, this will be postponed until when we really start with the Initial Appearance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SOLLEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I give you permission to -- Just before he walks in, I want his lawyer to inform him of what is -- what is happening. Does he understand any English at all or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. SOLLEY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you need someone to assist you in interpretation?

utterances.speaker: MR. SOLLEY
utterances.text: I would hope that if I were to call him in, he would come in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SOLLEY
utterances.text: -- without --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So do that, Mr. Solley --

utterances.speaker: MR. SOLLEY
utterances.text: If you permit me to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- and we will be forever grateful. Thank you. And Ms. Martinez, I suggest that perhaps if you can contact Mr. Pimentel, ask him to be present. Oh, I am sorry, Mr. Pimentel. I didn't notice your presence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Sljivancanin. THE ACCUSED SLJIVANCANIN: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the accused, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your microphone. Please take a chair. THE ACCUSED SLJIVANCANIN: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We haven't started the Initial Appearance as yet, and I don't think we will start it today, considering what has been submitted on your behalf by your capable lawyer here, who has been assigned to you for today's sitting. I am going to try and explain to you what is happening, because you have a right to know. Mr. Solley informed the Tribunal, informed me, actually, as soon as we started the sitting that two or three lawyers of your choice had asked the Tribunal to appoint them as your legal representatives and that they had contacted the Tribunal nine days ago and had not received any communications from the Tribunal until they themselves had to contact the Tribunal again, and that because of that, you were showing a preference to be represented today by lawyers who had indicated to this Tribunal that they are interested in taking over your legal representation. I agreed then and for some time that you could stay outside, waiting, while this was being investigated. I also told Mr. Solley to explain to you that I am the Presiding Judge and my function is not to accuse you, but my function is to make sure that our law is observed and that your rights are fully protected, and so I suspended this sitting and I instructed the Registry to make its own investigations to see exactly what happened in these last nine days and what the position was. I also told Mr. Solley to explain to you that the right to be represented by a lawyer of your own choice is not absolute or as absolute as you may think it is. You cannot, for example, choose to have half a dozen lawyers come here to represent you at the expense of the Tribunal with the Tribunal having no choice at all to decide whether they should represent you or not. We have got our own Rules. Those Rules are applied by the Registrar, and I myself as a Judge have no right to interfere with the discretionary powers that the Registrar has in these regards. I have other powers, powers to make sure that your rights are protected, but not to decide for and instead of the Registrar. I have a representative of the Registrar here present in the courtroom, a high official in the Registry, and I am going to ask him now to explain in your presence what happened. And after that -- I don't know what he's going to say, but after hearing him, then I will take a decision on how best to proceed according to our Rules and in a way in which your rights will not be even minimally violated. So Mr. Pimentel, you heard what Ms. Martinez had to say. Perhaps you are in a position to explain to the Chamber in greater detail what happened and what the position is now and how is it likely to develop so that we do not live on false illusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PIMENTEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. My name is David Pimentel. I am the chief of Court Management at the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. As is already entered in the record but for the benefit of the accused and at the request of the Court, let me summarise what has happened that leads us to this point. The attorneys in question -- the attorneys from Belgrade did fax to us last week - on Tuesday of last week - some basic information, including a summary of the experience of one of the attorneys and a request for assistance in obtaining visas. That assistance was given by Tribunal staff, but -- and powers -- a power of attorney proxy was submitted as well. It is the practice of the Tribunal not to accept such proxies from the attorney itself -- from attorneys themselves but to accept them from the accused. And at the time this was -- these documents were received, we had not -- the accused was not yet here, we had not yet had a chance to meet with the accused. The request of these attorneys to appear and represent the accused was not adequately communicated within our office. That is the -- I accept full responsibility for the oversight of staff that it was not acted upon in a timely way. We did receive new copies of these materials this morning. We realised that there had been some kind of oversight by yesterday and made repeated attempts to contact the counsel using mobile numbers that had been provided to us but were unsuccessful in making contact with counsel. Consistent with the practice of the Tribunal, in order to protect the rights of an accused, we appointed -- assigned, rather, a counsel who is here to represent and protect the rights of the accused for purposes solely of the Initial Appearance. I might add that what -- we took this action having viewed the CV that was submitted from which we could not ascertain that any of the -- either of the attorneys - I think there are three individuals named. One was an interpreter. There's been some confusion in record about whether there were two or three attorneys. I think there were two attorneys and an interpreter is my understanding of it. But it did not appear that the attorneys speak a language of the Tribunal, which is a requirement and prerequisite for assignment as counsel under Rule 44(A). Before assigning counsel, it is necessary for the Registry to confirm that all qualifications are met, not only the language requirement but also adequate experience in criminal law and a familiarity with proceedings, similar proceedings sufficient to ensure that the rights of the accused are protected. The Registry acted at all times, based on the information that we had, out of a desire to protect the rights of the accused and is, as a matter of policy, slow to appoint counsel and reluctant to appoint counsel until all of these things can be confirmed, and for this reason Mr. Solley was chosen as someone whose abilities were not in question. It does appear -- we've confirmed this morning that the proposed counsel do not speak a language of the Tribunal, at least not adequately well for the purposes of the Tribunal. While the Rules do, under Rule 44(B), allow an exception to be made to the language requirement, it is done under exceptional circumstances and in -- solely in the interest of justice and subject to such other conditions as may be imposed by the Registrar. And this is -- the granting of such exceptions is a matter of some sensitivity within the Tribunal. Now that we have located all the documents and been fully informed as to the current situation, we will -- the Registry will attempt to confirm the qualifications and to determine if there are exceptional circumstances in this case to justify the granting of an exception and the appointment of counsel who do not speak a language of the Tribunal. At this point, we have, even with the CV that has been submitted, we don't have sufficient information to verify the necessary experience and qualifications and we do not have any submission to suggest that exceptional circumstances exist. And so at this time it -- it does not appear likely that the Registry will be able to make such an exception, but that depends on what is submitted in the near future, and I presume something will be submitted along these lines. And also, as far as timing - this was alluded to earlier in this session - how long would it take the Registry to confirm qualifications, that depends on the cooperation that we receive from the proposed counsel in terms of providing us information that we need to verify their experience and to justify the finding of any exceptional circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you, Mr. Pimentel. Mr. Wubben, did you consult with your Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. For the record, my name is Jan Wubben, senior trial attorney, and I am accompanied with lawyers Mr. Mark McKeon, Ms. Joanne Richardson, and Ms. Kristina Carey, together with case manager Mr. David Bruff. Your Honour, the position of the OTP is that the accused is now under the complete authority of the Court as a detainee and in that position, of course, he should abide by the Rules and is not in a position to set any conditions. Whenever it is a condition of assigning of counsel, indigent counsel, meaning that if he doesn't abide with an assignment of the counsel who now appears on behalf of the accused - and I notified that you yourself, Your Honour, qualified this counsel who appeared today as a capable lawyer - then it means that refusal to abide with this counsel, with this assignment by the Registrar, means a kind of waiver. And so far there might be a kind of waiver, but the accused didn't specify that and didn't give an unconditional waiver of his right to be assigned by such counsel. As being informed by the Registrar, Your Honour, the OTP takes the position that it is up to the Registrar to decide, and we will take no position in that ourself. So we fully respect that. And from the beginning, as I state to you, it means that the accused is under the complete authority of this Court and the Rules, and the Rules demand that there will be an appearance before a Judge and that he will be fully charged. So that brings us to the conclusion that a delay of seven days or up to next week is not right and should be refused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Solley.

utterances.speaker: MR. SOLLEY
utterances.text: It seems, with respect, that once the Registrar had said what he'd said, and looking at Rule 44(B), and the last line in particular, which is that: "The suspect or accused may appeal a decision of the Registrar to the President," in order to make that a right which he may properly exercise, with respect, Your Honour, there can be little alternative but to a short delay, (A), to ensure that, as the Registrar put it, that they approach their task judicially; and (B), so that there can be consideration of an appeal, because until those rights are exhausted, technically speaking, the Rules haven't been followed. But I think, Your Honour, you understand the position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. And the position is quite clear in my mind. And my decision is as follows: I know that I can, technically speaking, today, irrespective of what has happened or what has not happened inside the Registry, that I am perfectly entitled, if I wanted to, to proceed with the Initial Appearance today since you are lawfully and properly appointed and everything else is in order. However, I have been taught from the very first day when I became a judge in my own country that the law unaccompanied by humanity sometimes can easily end up with making mistakes. So what I am going to do is that I am going to take a decision which hopefully will make your client understand that this is a serious court, Tribunal, that has no interest at all in bringing to your client more frustration than what he definitely is going through at this moment, two days after his arrival here in The Hague. So my decision is mostly motivated by a humanitarian reason more than by a legal reason. I am going to delay the Initial Appearance to Thursday of next week - that's today week - if necessary, also to Friday, but for the time being to Thursday of next week, by which time hopefully the Registrar should have cleared up this matter and come to a decision. But I also want to make it clear to your client here that if the Registrar comes to a conclusion that neither of the two lawyers that have asked to be appointed as his representatives are indeed accepted by the Registrar, and you retain your assignment as his counsel for the purposes of the Initial Appearance, at least, then today week I will proceed with the Initial Appearance. The Initial Appearance basically is one very important step in the whole course of the proceedings that have been instituted against your client. Other sittings following the initial proceedings, if he wants to -- if he wants to stay in the detention centre unit, he can stay there, it will not be any problem for me, but for the Initial Appearance, he needs to be here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SOLLEY
utterances.text: I don't anticipate a problem. Forgive my rudeness in not standing up when you were addressing me. I knew you were but I thought that your direct line of sight might be useful to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He is not the first high army officer that I have had to deal with in my career, and I consider high army officers as officers and gentlemen too, so I hope that your client will behave accordingly. The Initial Appearance will take place as I said -- Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I take it that a delay of the Initial Appearance will also mean that the transfer of the supporting, the confirming material, will also -- should also be delayed? Because we have now the supporting material with us. We can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can -- the handing over of the supporting material does not necessarily depend on whether the Initial Appearance takes place today or afterwards. I mean, if I were you, I would -- I would just hand it over and get it over and done with.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: We will hand it over to the accused. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Had we proceeded further, Colonel, today I would have explained precisely what your rights are and how they will be protected. However, that will be explained to you the next time you will come -- you will attend here in this courtroom, which will be next week. I can also inform you that by then probably there would be a revised, amended indictment. I don't know. I think you ought to know this, that the indictment, on the basis of which he has been detained and brought here is an old indictment, which is in the course of being amended. You know that initially they were four; now they are three. There is already a decision that goes back to roughly a year ago which made it clear that the three accused, Mrksic, Radic, and your client will be joined together as far as the trial is concerned. There's only going to be one trial. I am the Pre-Trial Judge in the case of the other two accused, Mrksic and Radic. I had a Status Conference, a conference yesterday. And eventually, for the next Status Conference, your client will be joined with them. He will -- he will join them. But there is in the process a -- an amended indictment. So what he will be pleading to probably will be the original indictment, but we will immediately -- almost immediately after come to an amended indictment, which will contain less charges and somewhat different charges as well. All right?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Just to make it clear, and in addition to your information, I confirm to you that there will be a new indictment, it will be an amended indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I can't get into details for less or more charges, but what I can say, that it will be filed before or on the 21st of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. That is an agreement we have and we -- which we confirmed yesterday during the Status Conference. I am going to address your client indirectly through you, Mr. Solley, even though we are not proceeding with the Initial Appearance today. It is the practice of the Judge conducting the pre-trial -- the Initial Appearance and also the Pre-Trial Judge during the whole process of the pre-trial stage and during Pre-Trial Status Conferences to enquire from and with the accused about his state of health, mental and physical, and also about the state of his detention. I want to convey to your client a message loud and clear that he has a right, while he is being detained in Scheveningen Detention Unit, to have his health properly looked after. And if that -- his reason for him to complain about that or to make any representations in regard, he is to feel free to let me know. That's number one. Secondly, the same thing, but I don't have any reason to suspect that this will ever happen: If he has a reason to complain about the conditions of detention, also please ask him to feel free to contact me and I will look into the matters promptly and efficiently. This is something that we communicate to all detainees over there and something which we check upon, and that's one of the reasons why we have periodical Status Conferences. I hope he is receiving proper interpretation, in his own language. I hope he has understood me. THE ACCUSED SLJIVANCANIN: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have understood everything you said. May I say something now too?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Mr. Sljivancanin. THE ACCUSED SLJIVANCANIN: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I respect all that you said. On the basis of the documents I received after my arrival in the Detention Unit in Scheveningen, I already studied the matter in Belgrade and some 20 days ago I selected lawyers who I believed could represent me during the Initial Appearance. I did not ask either for a delay or anything that will be contrary to the Rules. And now all of a sudden, when I arrived to the Tribunal, Mr. Solley turned up. I have never seen him before, and I simply did not want him to represent me, because I think that my rights as the accused are in jeopardy today. I think, and I have agreed with the lawyers, that if they see that something is wrong with these lawyers, that they will tell them and that they will deny them and withdraw my power of attorney that I gave them. But I wanted to appear today before the Court. I indeed wanted it. You were addressing Mr. Solley. I have not yet chosen him as my counsel for the time being. I have two counsel of my own choice. Of course, I have to respect all the decisions that the Tribunal is passing, but please allow me to make use of my rights and to enjoy the same rights as everybody else. Your Statute says that there is an equality of arms on all sides before this Court. I will respect the decisions that you take. You said that you hold in high regard high-ranked officers. I am an educated man, I understand all that you said, but I'm entitled to defend myself and to choose lawyers who I deem to be the best. If the Registrar of this Tribunal manages to persuade me that they are not, perhaps I will change my decision. But yesterday I explained that during the interview that we had; I said that the lawyers had arrived. I gave them telephone numbers. Yesterday I spoke to him five times. I could reach them whenever I wanted. I told them the problems that I had, and they said that they were coming and that they would manage to reach an understanding. I simply do not understand this, and why was I brought in this unenviable position in difference with all the others? Because it is my right to choose my lawyer, of course, with fully respecting the Rules. But if I chose bad lawyers, then my defence will be bad, and I believe, however, that the Court will pass honourable and correct decisions. I do not want to tax your patience any longer, but please allow me to choose the lawyers myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Sljivancanin, please take a chair. THE ACCUSED SLJIVANCANIN: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As I tried to explain to you, the choice of counsel can take place in two ways: You can show a preference and then that preference is communicated to the Registrar. You can even pay your own lawyers, and in that case also the name of the lawyer who you intend to pay from your own pocket will be communicated to the Registrar. But it is the Registrar who decides whether that lawyer will defend you or not. This is why I tried to explain to you that I as a Judge have got absolutely no right to replace the Registrar in the decision that needs to be taken with regard to the either appointment or assignment of counsel. We have had instances here of lawyers appointed by the Registrar and then sent back home, either because they were not capable or because we found out that there were instances in the past that would make it incompatible for them to represent anyone in this Tribunal. What I can assure you of is that the Registrar takes everything into consideration before taking -- reaching a decision. But the decision is reached by the Registrar and not by myself. The Rules also provide for a right of appeal, which you will have in case the Registrar decides against assigning the lawyer that you would like to have representing you. You have a right to appeal -- of appeal to the President of - that's not me - but the President of the Tribunal himself, and he has the final say in this. So this is why I'm trying to explain to you what your rights are. And I also invite you to make a distinction between the Initial Appearance and other stages of the proceedings, and I can inform you that since the Initial Appearance usually takes place pretty soon after the arrival of the accused, of the indicted person, into The Hague, most of the time - and almost always - the lawyer who is appointed to represent the accused for the purposes of the Initial Appearance is a lawyer who's never seen the face of his client. This is how it is here. Then there are certain safeguards that the Statute and the Rules provide for which would make it possible for you to remain silent, not to enter a plea, and you will be given time, by which time perhaps you will have proper counsel assigned to you for the purposes of the subsequent stages, and then you will enter a plea if you want to enter a plea. If you don't want to enter a plea, then I will enter it on your behalf, and I will plead not guilty on your behalf. But that's how the proceedings go. So my decision, as I tried to explain to you today, is I feel that at the present moment I should not proceed with the Initial Appearance since a decision has not really been taken with regard to the lawyers that you would have preferred to have here with you today, knowing that this decision wasn't taken when it could have perhaps been taken. So because of that and simply because of that, and to give you the opportunity to know where you stand, I am going to put off the Initial Appearance for seven days, for next week, by which time the situation should have crystallised. If we are still where we stand today, or worse still, if by then you would have received communication from the Registrar that they cannot appoint either of the two lawyers that were referred to before, then we will proceed with the Initial Appearance and I will safeguard your rights, leaving it until later to enter a plea. I will give you every right to remain silent and time within which you can then think it over and enter a plea and time within which you can appeal against the decision of the Registrar if the decision of the Registrar is against you, because it could well be in your favour. But let me make it clear to you: If you are expecting that as from now you will be assigned two lawyers, you might as well forget it. I am dealing with a trial that has been going on for a year and a half where I personally believe there should be more lawyers in the Defence, or at least the presence of more lawyers would make the task of the Defence much lighter than it is, and there is only one lead counsel with a co-counsel assisting. And that's the trial stage. At the pre-trial stage, I know very few cases, if at all, where you have lead counsel and also a co-counsel, let alone two counsels of the same standing. So I am making that clear, because I would imagine that although you would have already obtained some information about this Tribunal and how things go here, I'm pretty sure that you don't know or you're not aware of the whole -- of the whole scenario, and I am just explaining it to you. I mean, if you want to pay for lawyers out of your own pocket to come here, provided they have got the okay from the Registrar, I suppose you can -- you can have them, but don't expect the Registrar to appoint more than one lawyer to represent you, especially for the purpose of this pre-trial stage, unless there is, of course, other compelling reasons to go beyond one counsel and to appoint more than one. So we'll leave it at that. Yes, Mr. Solley.

utterances.speaker: MR. SOLLEY
utterances.text: I merely wish to thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SOLLEY
utterances.text: So if you rise now, it will give the lawyers an opportunity to speak to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I thank you, and we'll have the Initial Appearance next time, when everything is in order and the accused is feeling a little bit more tranquil and not feeling as if he has been abused by -- or disregarded. So we'll meet again today week.

utterances.speaker: MR. SOLLEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The time will be communicated, because I don't know if I'm sitting in the morning or I'm sitting in the afternoon next week. So to tell you the truth, I can't remember. And we will have it either Thursday, and if it's not possible Thursday, we'll have the Initial Appearance on Friday. In the meantime, try to keep in contact with your client and the Registrar will try and finalise the matter about representation. Thank you.
